intro: The Scherzo of Mahler’s Fifth Symphony, marked Kräftig, nicht zu schnell, is the large central dance movement of the work and has a solo horn part. Country Ländler and Viennese waltz overlap, then both stop for a horn call.

sections.label: A · Horn call and country dance
sections.mNote: Solo horn, woodwinds and violins take the tune in turn.

sections.label: B · Violin waltz theme in B♭
A′ · The opening call returns
sections.mNote: The call returns, followed by fast string entries.

sections.label: C · Long horn solo
sections.mNote: Long horn phrases, then quiet exchanges in plucked strings.

sections.label: Dev · Brass figures and running strings
sections.mNote: The dance tunes appear close together before the opening returns.

sections.label: A″ · The D major dance returns
sections.mNote: Old tunes combined with new string runs and wind replies.

sections.label: C′ · Obbligato horn solo returns
sections.mNote: The obbligato horn plays its long phrase again.

sections.label: Coda · Running strings and horn calls
sections.mNote: Dotted calls and running scales lead to two short chords.

cues.title: Opening, corno obbligato
cues.text: The horns open the movement with three notes. Mahler writes a separate corno obbligato part for one player. Marked Kräftig, nicht zu schnell — vigorous, not too fast — in three-four and D major, the opening passes its tune between the solo horn, the woodwinds and the first violins.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 118: Kräftig, nicht zu schnell; D major, 3/4; a separate staff for Corno obligato in F beside the four horns, whose first bars rise in three-note gestures. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide has a playful tune delicately tossed between a solo French horn, the woodwinds and the first violins: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler on the scherzo
cues.text: Natalie Bauer-Lechner reported Mahler’s idea for the scherzo: “a human being in the full light of day, in the prime of his life”. In the Fifth it follows the funeral march and the storm.
cues.evidence: The Aspen Music Festival programme note gives Bauer-Lechner’s report of Mahler’s idea for the character of the scherzo: https://www.aspenmusicfestival.com/program_notes/view/mahler-symphony-no.-5-in-c-sharp-minor . Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide quotes Mahler to Bauer-Lechner on 25 July 1901 about the same movement (“a human being in the full light of day”): https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/

cues.title: First trio, first violins
cues.text: At Etwas ruhiger (a little calmer) the first violins play a softer waltz in B♭ major over a largely pizzicato accompaniment. Mahler’s footnote asks for the eighth note in the motive to be played always a little fleetingly, a little carelessly.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 128, rehearsal 6: Etwas ruhiger; two flats; first violins carry the tune over pizzicato violas and basses; footnote “In diesem Motiv ist das Achtel stets etwas flüchtig-nachlässig auszuführen”. Basinger: the first trio is a clear waltz, a relaxed passage with a temporary relaxation of tempo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Horn call and fugato
cues.text: The opening horn call returns at fff and breaks off the waltz. A string fugato follows, with each entry starting before the previous line has finished, and Mahler marks wild! over the entries.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 132, rehearsal 8: horn call fff, then the running figure entering in violins, violas, cellos and basses, with wild! over successive entries. Basinger: the scherzo leads to a brief yet brisk fugue that ushers in the second trio: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Conversation with Natalie Bauer-Lechner, 1901
cues.text: In March 1901, while recovering from surgery, Mahler told Natalie Bauer-Lechner of his dream of themes that “develop freely, side by side, each with its own impetus and purpose”.
cues.evidence: The Aspen Music Festival programme note reports the conversations with Natalie Bauer-Lechner in March 1901 and quotes the remark: https://www.aspenmusicfestival.com/program_notes/view/mahler-symphony-no.-5-in-c-sharp-minor

cues.title: Solo horn, Tempo (poco sostenuto)
cues.text: The solo horn plays a slow melody marked Tempo (poco sostenuto). Its phrases are marked lang and verklingend, dying away, and stop on fermatas while English horn, bass clarinet, bassoons and low strings reply.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 136–137: four horns with bells in the air (Schalltrichter in die Höhe), the obbligato horn with rit. and molto portamento, then Tempo (poco sostenuto) with lang and verklingend in the horn part and answering English horn, bass clarinet, bassoons, violas, cellos and basses. Basinger: the second trio’s rocking theme, most prominently in an unaccompanied horn solo: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Mahler and the Bach edition
cues.text: Mahler subscribed to the collected edition of Bach’s works. Counterpoint plays a larger part in the Fifth. In the scherzo the strings continue their own dance beneath the horn’s.
cues.evidence: Mahler Foundation, Symphony No. 5 introduction, on the Bach edition and the growing role of counterpoint in the scherzo and finale. https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-introduction/

cues.title: Pizzicato fragments, rehearsal 11
cues.text: At rehearsal 11, Molto moderato, solo violins, cellos and basses play fragments of the dance pizzicato.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 137, rehearsal 11: Molto moderato, violins, cellos and basses marked Solo pizz. Basinger: Mahler explores the second trio’s theme through variation and fragmentation: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second trio, wind solos
cues.text: In the second trio the music is divided among small groups. Oboe, bassoons, trumpet and tuba each play a solo marked p espress. over sustained strings and a timpani roll. The themes pass from group to group.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 140: oboe, bassoons, trumpet and tuba each marked p espress., long string notes and a timpani roll beneath. Basinger: Mahler sets the rocking theme against itself and amid materials from the first trio: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Alma, Cologne, 1904
cues.text: During rehearsals in Cologne in October 1904, Mahler wrote to Alma that conductors for the next fifty years “will all take it too fast and make nonsense of it”. He wished he could give the symphony “its first performance fifty years after my death”.
cues.evidence: Peoria Symphony Orchestra’s programme essay quotes Mahler’s letter to Alma written during the rehearsals for the première: https://peoriasymphony.org/digging-deeper-into-mahlers-fifth/ . The Mahler Foundation’s concert record for Cologne, 18 October 1904: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/locations/germany/cologne/1904-concert-cologne-18-10-1904/

cues.title: Scherzo theme in the minor
cues.text: The solo horn announces a new section. The scherzo theme returns in a minor key with four flats, gradually faster, louder and more thickly scored. Its shape takes on the contours of the first trio’s waltz.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 140–145: four flats, the obbligato horn entering f at the end of p. 140, the crescendo to p. 145. Basinger: the solo horn announces the new section; the scherzo melody in a minor key, gradually faster, loud and thicker, takes on the contours of the first trio’s waltz: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Nicht schleppen, running figure in the bass
cues.text: Mahler marked the page Nicht schleppen (don’t drag). Bassoons, trombones, tuba and basses repeat a short running figure while the trumpets play across it. Woodwinds trill and the glockenspiel plays above.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 145: Nicht schleppen; four flats; the running figure in bassoons, contrabassoon, trombones, tuba and basses, trumpets repeating a short figure, trills in flutes, oboes and clarinets, glockenspiel ff.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the scherzo, rehearsal 17
cues.text: After a sudden halt, at rehearsal 17 the key signature changes from four flats to D major and the opening horn call returns, marked poco rit. a tempo I. The scherzo’s material is recapitulated as at the start of the movement.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 148, rehearsal 17: change of key signature from four flats to two sharps, poco rit. a tempo I., horn call in the four horns and the obbligato horn. Basinger: after the sudden halt the composer starts to recapitulate the scherzo’s material as at the movement’s outset: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Obbligato horn solo, tempo changes
cues.text: The obbligato horn plays its long phrase again while the tempo changes around it: Langsam, a tempo (schnell), rit., a tempo. Over the horn’s line Mahler writes nicht zurückhalten! (don’t hold back). The strings play tremolo beneath.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 170: obbligato horn with nicht riten and nicht zurückhalten!, Langsam, a tempo (schnell), rit., a tempo; strings trem. Basinger: the coda brings back the rocking theme in another lengthy horn solo, after which a sudden increase in tempo hastens the scherzo to its end: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda from rehearsal 32
cues.text: At rehearsal 32 winds, brass and violins play dotted rhythms fff over running scales in violas, cellos and basses. The score is marked Sehr drängend bis zum Schluss (very pressing to the close). The movement ends on two short fff chords.
cues.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 176–177: rehearsal 32, dotted figures in woodwinds, horns, trumpets and violins, running scales in violas, cellos and basses; p. 177 Sehr drängend bis zum Schluss, last two bars two short fff chords. Basinger: a sudden increase in tempo hastens the scherzo to its end: https://usuo.org/explore/2015/10/mahler-5-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: B♭ major, with plucked strings
transitions.from: A · Horn call and country dance
transitions.to: B · Violin waltz theme in B♭
transitions.how: The dance breaks off, and horns and trumpets play calls that fall from ff to pp. At rehearsal 6, marked Etwas ruhiger, the key signature changes to two flats. The first violins begin the waltz over pizzicato violas and basses, and half the cellos play a separate line arco.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 128, rehearsal 6: calls in horns and trumpets ff to pp, Etwas ruhiger, two flats, pizzicato violas and basses, cellos die Hälfte arco.

transitions.title: Horn call returns before the fugato
transitions.from: B · Violin waltz theme in B♭
transitions.how: At rehearsal 8 the opening horn call returns at fff, and the dance resumes in D major. The running string figure then enters in one string part after another. Each entry is marked wild!, and the accompaniment becomes a fugato.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), p. 132, rehearsal 8: horn call fff, running figure in successive string entries marked wild!. Basinger: a brief yet brisk fugue.

transitions.title: Horn entries lead to slower tempo
transitions.how: Over fff string chords, the four horns enter one after another on the same held note, bells raised. The solo horn then takes the line, marked rit. and molto portamento, and the tempo slows to Tempo (poco sostenuto).
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 136–137: Schalltrichter in die Höhe in the four horns, fff string chords, obbligato horn rit. and molto portamento, Tempo (poco sostenuto).

transitions.title: Return to D major at rehearsal 17
transitions.from: Dev · Brass figures and running strings
transitions.to: A″ · The D major dance returns
transitions.how: The music stops at a breath mark. At rehearsal 17 the key signature changes from four flats to D major, and the opening horn call returns, marked poco rit. a tempo I.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 145–148: Nicht schleppen (p. 145), breath marks and the change of key signature at rehearsal 17 (p. 148). Basinger: a sudden halt, then the scherzo is recapitulated as at the outset.

transitions.title: Bass-drum roll and quicker tempo
transitions.to: Coda · Running strings and horn calls
transitions.how: The tempo quickens at a tempo (schnell) over a bass-drum roll and string tremolos. At rehearsal 32 the woodwinds, brass and violins play dotted rhythms over running scales in the lower strings. From the marking Sehr drängend bis zum Schluss the tempo presses forward to the end of the movement.
transitions.evidence: Peters score (IMSLP #111956), pp. 170–177: a tempo (schnell), bass-drum roll, string tremolos (p. 170); rehearsal 32 (p. 176); Sehr drängend bis zum Schluss (p. 177).

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, III, Peters study score, plate 9015
source.locator: Printed pp. 118–177. The separate obbligato horn leads the opening; p. 128 introduces the gentler waltz; pp. 136–142 give the horn and pizzicato episodes; pp. 172–177 bring back the dance figures.

timeline.note: The horn call leads into the obbligato horn’s dance, answered across the orchestra.
Violins lead the gentler waltz above bassoon and plucked strings.
The obbligato horn lengthens its phrase as the accompaniment drops out.
Pizzicato strings exchange fragments of the dance.
Woodwind melodies pass above changing groups of brass and strings.
The strings play separate dance lines beneath calls in the wind and brass.
Clarinets and horns exchange phrases as the strings begin moving again.
Horn calls and running strings lead the orchestra into the close.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
